She thought about the yellow blob, then about the painting she'd seen in her grandmother's studio, a face built from see-through layers, and a new idea took hold. Maybe you weren't supposed to get the skin right in one go. Maybe you started light, almost too light, and added darker washes on top, a little at a time.

She worked all afternoon, laying down the palest layer first, letting it dry, then adding shadow under Mattea's cheekbones with a slightly stronger mix. When she tried to rush and painted over a damp section, the colours bled into a bruise, and she had to blot it with a tissue and start that layer again. It was a dilemma: wait and lose time, or push on and ruin it. She learned to wait.

By evening the face looked like Mattea, if Mattea were made of sunlight. Aubrey held it up. "Is it done?"

Her grandmother put on her glasses, looked, and then did something unexpected. She turned the painting toward the window, tilted it, and pointed at a patch on the forehead that had dried patchy and uneven. "Almost," she said. "One more wash, even across the whole face, will tie it together."

"That'll make it darker."

"A little. That's how it works."

Aubrey mixed the wash, added water until it was barely tea-coloured, and swept it over the face in one steady pass. The patchy spot vanished into the whole. Tomorrow she would paint the eyes, the hardest part, and she wasn't even scared of it now. She set the portrait on the windowsill to dry, and Mattea's face looked back at her, waiting.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a warehouse that collects and stores large amounts of food, while a food pantry is the local place where people pick up food directly.
story:
Andrew pushed open the metal door of the big brick building on Delmore Street, expecting a line of hungry people stretching to the corner. He'd brought his volunteer slip from Ms. García's class, and he'd imagined handing cans to grateful strangers all morning. Instead he stood in a cavernous room stacked floor to ceiling with pallets of soup, rice, and peanut butter, and not a single customer anywhere. His friend Cayden was already there, tying an apron, looking just as confused.

"Where is everybody?" Andrew asked. "The sign outside said this is where we volunteer."

Cayden shrugged. "Maybe nobody's hungry today."

Andrew didn't buy that. He walked the length of the warehouse, past shelves labeled with numbers, past a forklift parked by the loading dock. If people needed food, they weren't getting it here, and the boxes kept moving somewhere. He noticed the pallets were shrink-wrapped and stamped with the names of neighborhoods, and a clipboard by the dock listed pickup times for vans from churches and schools all over the city. That gave him an idea, and ideas, his dad always said, needed testing.

"Let's verify it," he told Cayden. "We ask the guy with the clipboard where the food goes."

The volunteer coordinator, a wiry man named Merrick who looked about seventeen, laughed when they asked. "You thought people walked in off the street? No, this is a food bank. A food bank is a warehouse that collects and stores huge amounts of food. The places where people actually come pick up groceries are called food pantries, little ones all over town. We ship to them."

Andrew felt his face go warm. He'd had the whole thing backward. He'd pictured himself handing a can of beans to a kid his own age, and instead he was standing in a giant cupboard. For a second he wanted to quit and call his mom to pick him up.

But then Merrick pointed at a map covered in pins. "St. Anne's pantry runs out of boxes by noon every Saturday. Want to ride along?"

They rode in the van, and at St. Anne's Andrew finally got his line of people. He stacked cans on a folding table while a woman with two toddlers chose bread and oranges, and Cayden bagged apples so fast the bagger tore. Andrew had thought the warehouse work didn't count because nobody saw it. Now he understood that the van, the pantry, and his own hands were all one chain, and every link mattered, even the invisible ones.

When they got back, Merrick asked if they'd sign up again next month.

"Both Saturdays," Andrew said, and grabbed a pen.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: The U.S. agency NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day, and each 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time.
story:
Leo held up two shirts in the clothing store, one blue and one green, and asked Cora which one looked less terrible. She pointed at the blue, but her eyes had drifted to a rack near the register, where foam earplugs hung in little paper packets beside a card with tiny print. The card said that the U.S. agency NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day, and that each 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time.

"Eight hours seems like forever," Cora said. "Why would anyone need these?"

Leo did the math out loud, slowly, because the numbers implied something that surprised him. "Eighty-five decibels is eight hours. Eighty-eight is four. Ninety-one is two. It drops fast." He bought the shirt and, after standing there a moment longer, a packet of earplugs too. The cashier raised an eyebrow but said nothing.

On Saturday, the gym had been transformed into something almost distinct from the place where they ran laps, with streamers and a spinning light and a stage at one end holding giant speakers taller than Mr. Addo, who was standing nearby checking his clipboard. Leo, Cora, and Massimo planted themselves right in front of the speakers because that was where the cool kids stood, and Massimo insisted that closer meant better.

After twenty minutes, Leo noticed a faint ring in his ears, a strange fullness that did not fade when he swallowed. He pulled out his phone and opened a sound meter app he had downloaded the night before. It read 106. He watched the number for a minute, thinking. At that level, the safe time was not hours at all. Each step of 3 halved it again and again, until barely any minutes were left.

"We need to move," he said. "Now, actually."

Massimo groaned, but Cora, who had been pressing a finger against her ear, grabbed his sleeve. The three of them walked to the middle of the gym, and Leo checked the app again. The reading had dropped by more than half. He handed the earplugs to Cora, kept one pair for himself, and offered the last to Massimo, who took it only after the bass hit so hard it rattled the bleachers.

Mr. Addo wandered over during a slow song and glanced at the foam in Leo's ears. "Smart," he said, and tapped his own ear, where a bit of orange foam was already visible.

From across the gym, Massimo shouted over the music, "Best spot in the whole place, and I found it first."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: In Excel, a 'bar chart' has horizontal bars and a 'column chart' has vertical bars, although both compare amounts across categories.
story:
Anthony's plan for the weekend was simple: prove to his dad that his screen time had actually gone down in October, so the November limit should go up. He needed numbers and a chart, because his dad trusted charts the way other dads trusted weather reports. Alek and Imran came over on Saturday with a bag of chips and the family laptop, and the three of them spread out on the living room rug in front of the coffee table.

"Week one, four hours," Anthony read off his notebook. "Week two, three and a half. Week three, three." Imran typed the numbers into a spreadsheet while Alek held the chip bag like a referee holding a whistle. In the empty cell under the column, Anthony typed his first formula, =SUM(B2:B5), and pressed Enter. The number 13 appeared instantly. Alek leaned over and squinted at it.

"That can't be right," Alek said. "Add it by hand." Anthony did, scribbling on the back of a chip receipt, and the total matched. The formula had counted something they couldn't see happening, all four weeks at once, and Anthony felt the laptop almost radiate importance in his hands. The living room lamp hummed. Somewhere the radiator ticked like a brittle stick.

Then came the chart. Anthony highlighted the weeks and the hours, clicked Insert, chose the first option that said Bar Chart, and hit Enter again. The chart appeared with the bars lying flat, sideways, week names running up the side instead of along the bottom. "It's broken," Anthony said. "It came out sideways." He was about to close the whole file and start over when Imran grabbed his wrist.

"Wait. Look at the other buttons." Next to Bar Chart there was a button labeled Column Chart, and its little picture showed upright bars. Anthony clicked it, and the same numbers stood up into vertical columns, neat as fence posts. He looked between the two thumbnails for a long moment, comparing. "Okay," he said slowly. "So in Excel a bar chart has horizontal bars and a column chart has vertical bars. They're both comparing amounts across categories. I picked the sideways kind on purpose. Sort of." Alek laughed so hard a chip flew out of the bag.

On Sunday, Anthony showed his dad the printout, columns climbing left to right, total of thirteen hours in bold at the bottom. He had also added a new factor to his argument: a second column for homework hours, which had gone up. His dad studied the chart, tapped the total, and said he'd think about the limit. Then he asked, quietly, whether the spreadsheet could do the household budget too. Anthony pulled the laptop back onto his knees and said, "Sit down. This is going to take a formula."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Moving the horizon line up or down changes the view: a low horizon makes the street feel seen from a child's height, a high one from a window above.
story:
Declan pushed his drawing of Main Street across the kitchen table and waited while Avianna held it up to the light, the way Mr. Ma did in art class when he wanted to check whether the lines were true. The assignment was due tomorrow: a street drawn in one-point perspective, every edge aimed at a single vanishing point. Declan had tried three times, and every time the buildings looked like they were falling over sideways.

"Your vanishing point wanders," Avianna said, tapping the spot where the two sides of the street were supposed to meet. "Here it's in one place, and here it's somewhere else. My brother says your pencil rebels if you don't anchor it, you have to pin the point first and make every line obey it."

So Declan drew a small dot in the middle of a fresh sheet and refused to let it move. He lined his ruler up so the curb, the rooftops, the shop windows, and even the stripes on the candy shop awning all pointed at the dot like roads on a map. Slowly the flat paper deepened into a street you felt you could walk down. Avianna, working beside him on her own drawing of the same street, kept glancing at his page and frowning.

"Ours don't match," she said. "Same street, same dot in the middle, but yours looks like the view from the curb and mine looks like the view from the upstairs window of the bakery."

Declan leaned over. She was right. In his drawing, the pavement took up most of the page, tall building faces rising above it. In hers, the street was a thin ribbon squeezed down at the bottom, and you could see the rooftops flat against the sky, with a dry, arid stretch of gravel roof where the bakery's gutters ran. They argued about who had it wrong until Declan noticed something. His horizon line, the flat line running through the vanishing point, sat low on his page. Hers sat high.

"Wait," he said. He grabbed a new sheet, folded it in half to mark the middle, and drew the same street twice: once with the horizon pushed down near the bottom, once with it lifted almost to the top. The low one felt like the street seen from a kid's height, the way it looked when he sat on the curb outside the candy shop. The high one felt like looking down from a window above.

"You sat on the curb when you sketched it," he told Avianna, "and I stood at the bakery window upstairs, remember? Our eyes were at different heights." He flipped his folded sheet over and showed her the two versions side by side. "Mr. Ma is going to lose his mind. We could start a guild, the Horizon Movers, and do the whole class assignment from every floor of every building on Main Street."

Avianna laughed so hard she nearly knocked over the pencil jar, and then she bent over her page and drew a tiny figure sitting on her curb, right at the bottom of the street, waving up at the window.

"There," she said. "Now put me in yours. Window seat, third floor, and I'm holding a cinnamon roll."

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: A chapati cooks on a hot, dry griddle in only a minute or two, which is why flatbreads are usually made last.
story:
Ellie stood at the steel counter in the back of her family's restaurant, rubbing flour between her fingers while the lunch rush rattled the dining room on the other side of the wall. Ms. Nur, who had run this kitchen for eleven years, had put her in charge of one whole meal today: rice, a pot of curry, and a stack of chapatis. "Everything ready at the same time," Ms. Nur had said. "That is the whole trick of cooking. A hungry consumer does not wait." Ellie had nodded like she understood, and she had decided to start with the flatbreads, because they looked like the hardest part.

She rolled and cooked the chapatis first, one after another, laying them on a plate in a neat tower. The rice went on next, then the curry, which needed to bubble for a long while. She stirred it, tasted it, and stirred it again. When the curry was finally thick and fragrant and the rice soft, she carried all three dishes to the pass, proud and ready. Ms. Nur picked up a chapati and bent it. It cracked in half with a dry snap, stiff as a plate.

Ellie frowned at the broken bread. She had watched Ms. Nur make chapatis before, and they were always soft and folded. She tried to remember the order of things on those days. The curry had always been already simmering, the rice already steaming, and Ms. Nur would stand at the griddle at the very end, flipping bread while waiters hovered. That was the pattern. The flatbreads were last, every single time. Ellie looked at the griddle, hot and dry and empty, and thought about how quickly each round of dough had puffed and browned when Ms. Nur cooked it. A minute, maybe two, and it was done.

"The chapatis are no good," Ellie said. "I made them first."

"Then make them again," said Ms. Nur, and turned back to the fryer without another word. It was not a scolding. It was permission.

Ellie mixed fresh dough, rolled it thin, and waited. She let the curry simmer and kept the rice warm, and only when an order came in did she slap a circle of dough onto the dry griddle. It blistered and puffed in under a minute, and she flipped it, counted to ten, and slid it steaming onto the plate beside the curry. The second one took even less time. Luciana, wiping tables on the other side of the pass, leaned over and sniffed. "That smells exceptional," she said. "Can I be your first customer?"

Ellie tore a warm chapati, dipped it into the curry, and set the plate on the pass. "One order," she said, "rice, curry, and bread, all hot at once." Luciana picked it up and carried it out through the swinging door.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: A paper tissue left in a pocket breaks apart in the wash and scatters white shreds over every item in the load, which is why pockets are checked before washing.
story:
Christopher stood in the laundry aisle of Mr. Takahashi's grocery store, holding a bottle of detergent like it might explode. His mother had finally declared that he was old enough to do his own laundry, and she had sent him here with a short list and a shorter explanation.

"Get the kind with the blue cap," she'd said. That was it. No hints about what to do if the blue cap came in six varieties.

"You look like you're choosing a car," said Tessa, appearing beside him with her own basket. She and Bruno had come for snacks, but they found Christopher's suffering more entertaining.

"There are too many choices," Christopher said. "This one converts hard water. This one fights odours. What if my clothes have both hard water and odours?"

"Bold of you to assume anyone can tell," Bruno said, dropping two bags of chips into Tessa's basket.

Christopher took the cheapest blue-capped bottle, feeling he'd won a small battle, and the three of them walked to the checkout where Mr. Takahashi worked the register on Sundays. The store was strangely tranquil, just the hum of the coolers and a radio playing somewhere in the back.

"First load?" Mr. Takahashi asked, scanning the detergent. "You have the face of a boy about to learn something."

"Everyone keeps saying that," Christopher muttered.

At home, he sorted his clothes into piles, darks and lights, the way his mother had described. He checked one or two pockets, found a pencil in a hoodie, and felt proud of his thoroughness. Then he shoved everything dark into the machine, dumped in detergent, and pressed start. He watched the drum spin for a while, like a slow carnival ride, then went to fold his other laundry.

Forty minutes later he opened the machine and stared. Every dark shirt, every pair of jeans, every sock was speckled with white, as though a snowstorm had happened inside the drum. He pulled out his favourite black hoodie and it looked like a negative of the night sky.

He dug through the wet pile and found the culprit: the shredded remains of a paper tissue, dissolved and scattered across everything. One tissue. From one pocket. The pockets he hadn't checked.

He called Tessa. "I checked some pockets," he said. "Some is not enough."

"New consensus: check every pocket," she said, and he could hear Bruno laughing in the background.

Christopher picked the shreds off piece by piece, then ran the load again with nothing in it but water, and most of the specks floated away. When his mother came home, he showed her the hoodie, only slightly snowy still.

"Every pocket," he said. "I'm checking every pocket, every time, forever."

His mother smiled. Christopher took his black hoodie upstairs and hung it on his door, speckles and all, like a flag.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Most travelers find jet lag harder to adjust to after flying east than after flying west.
story:
The minivan smelled like airport coffee and the orange peel her dad kept in the cup holder. Victoria sat in the back with her duffel between her feet, watching the highway lights slide past. They had spent nine days at her aunt's house in California, and the flight home had landed an hour ago. Her brother was already asleep against the window, but Victoria's whole body felt wrong, like her bones had stayed three hours behind in another time zone.

"Text me when you land!" she said out loud, remembering Parker's message. She pulled out her phone and typed: landed. feel like garbage. why??

Parker replied fast. weird, u were fine when u flew OUT there. Victoria stared at that. It was true. On the way west she had stayed up late, slept in, and felt normal by the second day. Now, flying east, she was exhausted at seven in the evening and wide awake at three in the morning. She scrolled through Parker's next messages. my mom says most travelers find jet lag harder to adjust to after flying east than after flying west. She read it twice. West had been easy. East was wrecking her.

"I'm boycotting the east," she announced to the car. "Direction, that is. When we fly again, we only go west."

"That would make an interesting family," her dad said, checking the mirror. "We'd have to become descendants of people who circled the globe forever." He signaled and changed lanes. "Your grandmother did that once, actually. Never came back east, if I remember right."

Victoria opened her notebook, the versatile little one she used for everything, lists, homework, bad drawings, and made two columns in the dark by the glow of her phone. WEST, she wrote, and under it: felt fine, stayed up later, easy. EAST: awful, awake at 3 a.m., took over a week. Parker's mom's rule fit both trips. It wasn't the airplane, and it wasn't the length of the flight, because both flights were about the same. It was the direction. She decided to test it, in her own small way. School started in two days, and she would keep a chart: what time she got sleepy, what time she woke up, every day, until her body caught up.

The car turned onto their street. Ahead, under the porch light, Ms. Chowdhury from next door was pulling her recycling bin in from the curb, and she raised a hand as they passed. Victoria's dad tapped the horn twice, a short friendly beep, and pulled into the driveway. Victoria grabbed her duffel, pushed the door open into the cold air, and said, "Dad, I need a wall calendar. Tomorrow. It's for science."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Relationship researcher John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which is about one specific action, from criticism, which attacks a person's character with words like 'you always' or 'you never'.
story:
The family group chat, labeled "Rivera Household," buzzed at 7:04 a.m. Adam's mom had posted a photo of two concert tickets with the caption "TONIGHT 7pm, me and Dad. Home by 10. Be nice to each other." Adam stared at his phone. Tyler, his best friend since third grade, was coming over at six so they could finish their science project before the deadline tomorrow, except Tyler probably wasn't coming, because they hadn't spoken since Saturday. Adam had sent a message that morning saying "You never keep secrets. You always tell Sam everything," and Tyler had replied with one thumbs down and nothing since.

All day at school Adam collected evidence like a detective. Tyler had, in fact, told Sam one secret, on Friday, one time. But Tyler had kept dozens of others, including the embarrassing one about the pool party in fifth grade. So Adam's message wasn't even true, which bothered him more than the fight itself. In Ms. Francis's class, while she wrote the science project rubric on the board, he flipped through his health textbook and found a page about a researcher named John Gottman. Gottman separates a complaint from criticism, the book said. A complaint targets one specific action. Criticism attacks a person's whole character, and it uses words like "you always" or "you never." Adam copied the page number into his notebook, 214, and underlined it twice.

At lunch Mina slid her tray across from his. "You look like a kid who found out his homework is due an hour early," she said.

"Kind of the opposite." He showed her the page. "I criticized Tyler instead of complaining. That's the word, criticism. A complaint is about one specific action, like 'you told Sam what I said on Friday.' But 'you never keep secrets' goes after who he is."

"So rewrite it," Mina said, shrugging. "You have until six, which is, what, four hours?"

"I also have to integrate his volcano results into the poster before then, which is a whole separate plague."

"Then stop sitting here being negligent about it and go find him," she said, and stole his fries.

The plague metaphor followed Adam through the halls, because eighth graders flooded every route to the gym. He caught Tyler at his locker before the final bell. "One sentence," Adam said. "You told Sam what I said on Friday, and it got back to me, and that's what I was actually mad about. Not 'always,' not 'never.' Just Friday."

Tyler shut his locker slowly. "Sam begged me for twenty minutes. I caved. I was going to tell you myself Saturday, but your message hit first and it stung."

"Fair. Can you still come at six? I can't integrate your lava data without you."

"I'll come at five," Tyler said. "Bring graph paper."

At 6:58, with the poster finished and leaning against the couch, Adam photographed it and dropped the picture into the family group chat with the message "Done. Volcano survives until tomorrow." His mom replied with a fire emoji, and Tyler handed him a marker to sign his name at the bottom.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, the single vanishing point is at Christ's head, and a nail hole Leonardo used to stretch his guide strings is still visible there.
story:
Brayden had erased his street so many times that the paper was starting to dissolve into gray smudge, and the drawing still looked like a pile of boxes falling downhill. He slumped at the kitchen table, pencil hovering. The assignment was due Monday, and Ms. Kerr had promised it would hang in the hallway outside the art room. His older sister got a drawing hung last year. Brayden wanted his up there too.

The doorbell rang twice, fast, which meant Kailyn. She came in holding her own attempt, a street of shops that somehow got wider as it went back, like the road was walking toward you. "It's broken," she announced. "Mine too," Brayden said. "Mine's so bad I almost recycled it, but then I'd have guilt about wasting paper, so I just stared at it instead."

They laid the drawings side by side. Brayden got the ruler out and ran it along the edges of his buildings, and that was when he saw it. All the lines that should slant, the rooftops, the curb, the shop window ledges, pointed the same wrong way, scattered like dropped chopsticks. "They're supposed to meet," he said slowly. "One point. Everything goes to one point." Kailyn leaned in. "Wait. My mom showed me a picture of this in a museum book. The Last Supper, the giant one by Leonardo da Vinci. The single vanishing point is at Christ's head." She tapped her drawing. "Every edge in that painting points right at him. And get this, there's a tiny nail hole at that exact spot, because Leonardo hammered in a nail and stretched guide strings from it, like spokes, to get his lines straight. The hole is still visible in the painting."

Brayden stared at her. "A nail hole in one of the most famous paintings on Earth? From string?" He grabbed a fresh sheet before the thought could dissolve. "That's it. That's the trick. You don't guess the lines, you build them from one point." He marked a dot at the top center of his page, then, feeling only slightly ridiculous, pressed the pencil point down like a nail. He drew a horizon line through it, laid his ruler from the dot to the bottom corner, and swept a street edge into place. Then another line, then another, all of them running obediently home to the dot.

Kailyn pulled her chair over so fast it banged his. "Do mine next, do mine." She marked her own vanishing point and started twisting her ruler toward it, tongue between her teeth. Her shops leaned backward at first, endangered by her enthusiasm, but she steadied the ruler with two fingers. Brayden added windows, shrinking each one smaller as it climbed toward the dot, and the flat paper suddenly had depth, a real street you could walk down.

They worked until the kitchen went gold with evening light, two streets racing toward two little dots. "Monday," Kailyn said, holding hers at arm's length. "Hallway, here we come." Brayden pressed his pencil tip once more onto the vanishing point, like a nail going in.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: A strong thesis makes a claim that a reasonable person could disagree with; a statement nobody would dispute, like a plain fact, gives an essay nothing to argue.
story:
"Nobody argues with 'Grandpa's garden has vegetables,'" Alexandre said, waving the paper at the porch table where Leila and Juan sat with lemonade. It was Friday at Grandpa's house, which had somehow become the meeting spot for their writing club, mostly because Grandpa's porch was cool and his dog, Mops, listened well.

Leila frowned at her draft. "It's a thesis. Mr. Iyer said a thesis goes at the end of the first paragraph." She had promised to email her essay to Mr. Iyer by Sunday night, and the new curriculum at school said everyone had to outline a three-point argument before drafting. Alexandre was there to help, and also because Grandpa had promised pie.

"Watch," Alexandre said, and turned to Grandpa, who was watering tomatoes. "Grandpa, your garden has vegetables. Agree or disagree?"

Grandpa squinted. "Agree. Plain as the nose on my face."

"See? Nobody could disagree. A statement nobody would dispute, like a plain fact, gives an essay nothing to argue." Alexandre tapped the paper. "Try a claim a reasonable person could argue against. Then you've got something."

Leila chewed her pencil. Juan, who was supposed to be outlining his own essay about the school's most influential athlete, leaned in. "What about 'Grandpa's garden is better than the farmers market'?"

"Grandpa could disagree with that," Leila said slowly. "The cashier at the market would too. Even my mom might." She grabbed a fresh sheet and started listing points: the tomatoes were fresher, the price was lower, and the drive was shorter. Three points. "That's an argument!"

Then came the twist. Grandpa set down the watering can and cleared his throat. "Fresher, maybe. Cheaper, sure. But the farmers market has a man who sells honey I cannot grow. So I, a reasonable person, disagree." He smiled like he'd just won something.

"That's perfect," Alexandre said. "If even one reasonable person can push back, the thesis works." He was so excited he knocked over the lemonade, and Mops licked it up before anyone could grab a towel.

Leila rewrote her first paragraph right there, reading it aloud while Juan took notes for his own outline. When she finished, she turned to Grandpa. "You're going in my rebuttal paragraph. You and your honey man."

"I'd be honored," Grandpa said. "Now, who wants pie before the market closes?"

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In James Hurst's 1960 story The Scarlet Ibis, a storm-blown red bird dies in the family garden, foreshadowing the fate of the fragile boy Doodle.
story:
Chase turned the photocopied pages of "The Scarlet Ibis" as the school bus rattled past the strip mall. Mr. Santos had promised a reading quiz first period, and the quiz asked one thing: find the foreshadowing and explain what it suggests. Chase could retell the plot fine, but spotting hidden clues inside it felt like trying to see wind.

Toby dropped into the seat across the aisle, unwrapping a granola bar. "You look like the bus ran over your homework."

"The quiz is on this story, and I can't find the clue everyone keeps saying is there." Chase tapped the page. "This brother is ashamed of Doodle, the little brother who can't walk, and then at the end something bad happens. But I can't see what's supposed to warn me."

Shay leaned over the seatback from behind. "Rewind. What shows up earlier that's red and fragile?"

Chase ran his thumb down the margins. There it was, a few pages before the end: a storm blows a scarlet ibis into the family garden, and the exotic red bird dies there in the yard. Doodle, small and fragile himself, buries it. He read the passage again while Toby's granola bar began to decompose into crumbs on the vinyl seat, and the pieces lined up. A red bird, broken by a storm, dies. Then a fragile boy is caught out in a storm too. "The bird," Chase said slowly. "The ibis is the foreshadowing. It's pointing at Doodle."

"That's the whole trick," Shay said. "The bird's not just a bird, it's standing in for him."

Chase tested it out loud, the way he'd have to write it on the quiz. "The dying scarlet ibis foreshadows Doodle's fate, because both are fragile, both are battered by a storm, and both are lost too soon." Saying it made it solid. He underlined the bird's death in pencil, then flipped back and underlined every mention of red: the bird, the bleeding tree, Doodle's name, the scarlet leaves.

"How'd you even get this fast?" Toby asked.

"My mom calls it the family curse," Shay said. "Thinks being bad at math is hereditary. She's wrong, but at least the phrase stuck." She grinned. "Same thing. Once you know what to look for, you see it everywhere. Mr. Santos will probably ask how the quiz revenue from the bake sale's doing, too, so study that order form."

The bus groaned around the last corner toward school. Chase folded the pages, wrote one word at the top of his notes, and slid the pencil behind his ear. "Storm-blown red bird," he said. "Got it."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Día de los Muertos, celebrated in Mexico mainly on November 1 and 2, honors family members who have died with home altars called ofrendas.
story:
Every November second, Taylor's grandmother turned the side table in her living room into something magical. She stacked wooden boxes into tiers, draped them with an embroidered cloth, and set out candles, marigolds, and little dishes of food until the whole corner glowed. Taylor had helped with the altar since she was seven, but this year she noticed something odd. Her grandmother always placed a bowl of her mother's favorite cuisine, tamales, near the top, and always positioned the candles so their light refracted through a glass of water and scattered orange patterns across the photo of Abuela Elena. But there was a second, smaller frame that went in the very back, turned so slightly toward the wall that you could barely see the face in it.

Taylor wanted to know who it was, and more than that, why it was hidden. Her grandmother never explained the back photo, and Taylor had learned that asking directly got her only a smile and a change of subject. So she tried an experiment. While her grandmother was in the kitchen rolling out dough for pan de muerto, Taylor slipped the frame forward and turned it to face the room.

The photo showed a young man in a soldier's uniform, maybe nineteen, with the same crooked grin as Taylor's grandmother. When her grandmother came back carrying the bread, she stopped in the doorway. She set the plate down slowly, then picked up the frame and held it near the window light.

"His name was Ruben," she said. "My brother. He died when I was twelve, and we didn't put his picture on the altar for many years, because it hurt too much to see it." She traced the edge of the frame with her thumb. "But the ofrenda is for honoring everyone we've lost, so one year I put him in the back, where I could visit him without everyone asking questions."

Taylor's friend Kyra arrived just then with her mother, carrying a jar of marigolds for the altar. Kyra's class had made one at school, and she was full of facts. "Our teacher said the celebration happens in Mexico mainly on November first and second," Kyra announced, "and that these home altars are called ofrendas." She peered at the soldier's photo. "Who's that?"

"My brother," Taylor's grandmother said, and this time she said it out loud, to a guest, without flinching. She set the frame in the front row, right beside Abuela Elena, and adjusted it until the candlelight reached his face.

Kyra's mother asked if they could light the candles together, and Taylor's grandmother handed Taylor the match.

"You do it," she said. "He should meet you properly."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Instant replay was first used in a live sports broadcast by CBS director Tony Verna during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963.
story:
The living room at Ms. Nolan's house was so crowded that John ended up on the floor with a paper plate of nachos balanced on his knee. The championship game had four minutes left, and the score was tied. Theoren sat on the arm of the couch, Rosemary claimed the beanbag chair, and Ms. Nolan's brother, whom everyone just called the uncle, had the best seat in the house and intended to keep it.

Then the running back dove for the goal line, the officials huddled, and everybody in the room winced at once. Touchdown or no touchdown? The referee's arms stayed at his sides while he talked into his headset, and the suspense was so thick that Theoren grabbed a cushion and held it like a shield. "They're checking the replay," Rosemary said. On the screen, the play appeared again, frozen, then run backward, then forward, and John noticed something odd.

He leaned toward the television. The clock in the corner of the picture read 3:41, but the game clock on the score graphic at the top still said 3:52. He nudged Theoren. "Look. Two clocks, two different times. The small one is inside the picture, so the picture itself has to be from before. It's a recording, not live." Theoren squinted, then pointed. "And the left tackle is standing in a different spot. That's the same play from a second ago."

"It's instant replay," the uncle said, without taking his eyes off the screen. "Want to hear something? The first time TV ever did that in a live sports broadcast was the Army-Navy football game, December 7, 1963. A CBS director named Tony Verna made it happen." John stared at him. "You mean before that, if you missed a play, you just missed it?" "For live sports, yes. It didn't exist."

The whistle blew, the referee raised both arms, and the room erupted. Nachos went everywhere. Rosemary jumped up so fast the beanbag chair rolled over Theoren, and the uncle did a lap around the coffee table, which Rosemary's little brother described later as a reckless move for a man his age. Then the kicker lined up for the extra point, and Ms. Nolan called from the kitchen that the pizza was arriving in exactly one minute.

"Hold the pizza," the uncle shouted, "hold everything." The ball snapped, the kick sailed through, and the camera cut to the crowd. A second later the same kick appeared again, from a different angle. "Replay," John said, pointing at the two mismatched clocks before the picture even started moving. "Told you." Theoren threw the cushion at him, and the doorbell rang.
